opening.headline: Learn the structure of Agent SDK, which uses Claude Code's functions in your app, and Agent Skills, which loads repetitive procedures only when necessary.
body: As you build your agent, you'll keep piling the same description into the system prompt. In most conversations, only a portion of the conversation is needed, but all of it occupies the context, and when you restart the process, your memory of the conversation up to that point is lost.

In this class, we'll explore agent loops, sessions, and subagents in the Agent SDK, and the structure and writing best practices of Agent Skills for escalating repetitive procedures to progressive disclosure. Next, we distinguish how skills and tools differ and explain examples of combining the three devices in one task.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain Agent SDK's loops, sessions, sub-agents, and Agent Skills
Can distinguish between skills and tools
You can explain that the skill is used by looking at the description, the model reads the file, and when you resume the session, the record goes back into the input.

screens.title: Agent pasting the same description every time
screens.lead: First, read the challenges faced by a team that created an in-house code review agent. As you read, try to distinguish which information you need all the time and which information you need only occasionally.

visual.alt: A scene showing memories lost due to a prolonged system prompt and restart.
labels: The way is blocked, you can't go back to the beginning

paragraphs: One team created an in-house code review agent. We put review procedures, report forms, and team rules all into system prompts, and the prompts got longer over time. In most conversations, only some of them are needed, but all of them take up context every time.

There is something more difficult. Upon restarting the process, the agent lost all previously read files and conclusions. You are halfway through a long analysis and have to start over from the beginning. Also, if you get stuck while trying one method, there is no way to go back to the beginning and try another method.

This scene is a mix of three different issues. These are the execution-based issues of running an agent in code, the memory issues of linking conversations, and the issues of when to put repeated procedures into context. If you try to solve all three problems with one tool, the system prompts will just keep getting longer.

The question this class asks is this. How to separately manage agent execution base, conversation memory, and iterative procedures. Claude's Agent SDK and Agent Skills each answer part of this question.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which review procedures, reporting forms, and team rules are always needed in every conversation, and which are needed only when a review is requested?

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had to copy and paste the same work instructions every time?
items.answer: If you have to copy and paste repeatedly, it is better to organize the instructions once and recall them when needed. Each time you paste it, it takes up context, and you run the risk of splitting versions and having different instructions running around.

items.prompt: Have you ever been interrupted in the middle of a long analysis, then restarted and repeated the previous part?
items.answer: You can continue as long as you have a record of the analysis, that is, the files you read and the decisions you made. A session is a device that records the agent's conversation on disk and retrieves it.

items.prompt: How was this problem similar to your experience creating job descriptions when welcoming new team members?
items.answer: If you give a new team member a work guide, they don't have to explain it from scratch every time, and they can turn to the chapters they need when they need it. The same thing works for agents. This analogy is directly in line with Skills’ design philosophy.

items.prompt: Which two devices will we cover in this lesson?
items.answer: It covers execution and memory provided by the Agent SDK, and Agent Skills that serve as a guide. The former is a way to run an agent in code, and the latter is a way to efficiently load an iterative procedure into a context.

screens.outro: First, let's look at what Agent SDK is and where it is used.

screens.title: Agent SDK Overview: Put Claude Code's agent in your app
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what Agent SDK is, how it differs from other options, and what features it has.

tabs.label: What is an agent?
tabs.body: An agent is an application that plans its own steps and calls tools such as reading files, executing commands, or modifying code to get the job done. Instead of directing each step, people decide their next actions by looking at the results.

tabs.label: Agent SDK
tabs.body: The Agent SDK allows tools like Claude Code, agent loops, and context management to be programmed in Python and TypeScript. If Claude Code is a terminal product, SDK is a way to use the engine within your app. To use the same loop in another language, simply run the CLI as a subprocess with the `-p` flag and `--output-format json`.

tabs.label: Distinction from other options
tabs.body: If you want to use it for everyday development in the terminal, the CLI is the way to go. In the client SDK that calls the API directly, I write the tool loop. The way Anthropic hosts its agents is Managed Agents. The criteria for distinction are where the loop runs and who operates it.

tabs.label: SDK features
tabs.body: There are built-in tools, and hooks allow me to run my code at set points in its life cycle. Subagents and MCPs can be used, and automatic execution and approval are distinguished by permission settings. Continue conversations with sessions and recall skills, commands, and memories.

screens.outro: Next, let's take a step-by-step look at the agent loop that the SDK runs.

screens.title: Agent Loop: From Prompt to Result
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the agent loop step by step.

steps.title: 1. Receive a prompt
steps.body: System prompts, tool definitions, and conversation history are passed to the model along with the prompts. Session metadata appears as the first message. Session metadata contains information such as the tool and model used for this run, allowing the app to confirm its launch.

steps.title: 2. Evaluate and respond
steps.body: The model evaluates the current state and responds in text or requests a tool call. One Assistant message appears for each content block. In some cases, text and tool calls are output together, so a single evaluation can be split into multiple blocks.

steps.title: 3. Run the tool
steps.body: Runs the requested tool and gathers the results. The results are returned to the next judgment. Hooks allow you to intercept, change, or block something before execution. Hooks are used at this point to block dangerous commands or modify input.

steps.title: 4. Repeat
steps.body: One cycle is one turn. This continues until a response without a tool call is issued. Simple questions can be completed in one or two turns, while complex tasks can take dozens of tool calls.

steps.title: 5. Return the result
steps.body: You will receive a resulting message containing the final text, token usage, cost, and session ID. The session ID is the key to continuing the conversation in the next step. Cost information allows the app to immediately record how much a single run costs.

screens.outro: Let's look at sessions, a way to continue the conversation.

screens.title: Sessions: Continue, Resume, Gala View
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can see what the session stores and how it continues or splits.

items.title: What is a session?
items.body: A session is a record of conversations accumulated by the SDK as the agent works. It contains prompts, all tool calls and results, and all responses, and is automatically written to disk. When you return, you carry over the files you've already read, the analyzes you've done, and the decisions you've made. This allows you to ask follow-up questions, recover from interruptions, and try different approaches.

items.title: continue
items.body: Finds and continues the most recent session in the current directory. It is suitable for apps that conduct one conversation at a time as it does not require a session ID.

items.title: resume
items.body: Inherit by specifying a specific session ID. This is necessary when there are multiple sessions per user or when you need to go back to a session that is not the most recent. The app must record the ID directly.

items.title: fork
items.body: Leave the original session as is and create a new session with a copy of that record to try another access. If your attempt fails, simply return to your original session. This is a solution to the problem of not being able to return to the original state at a dead end.

items.title: What Sessions Don't Store
items.body: What a session stores is conversations, not the file system. Files changed by the agent are restored separately using file checkpointing. Additionally, within a single `query()` call, the agent takes as many turns as necessary, and session management is necessary when multiple prompts need to share context.

items.title: Why you need a session and how much it costs to resume
items.body: The model only knows what it receives as input for each call. So the session stores the previous record and returns it as input for the next call. Resuming restores all context from the previous turn, so the longer the history, the longer the input the model must read when reopening. Remember, it's not because the model has memory, it's how the record is read back.

items.title: When context is full: automatic compression
items.body: The context window is not reset between turns and continuously accumulates system prompts, tool definitions, conversation history, and tool input/output. When the window approaches its limit, the SDK automatically compresses old entries by summarizing them, freeing up space while preserving recent exchanges and key decisions. Upon compression, a `compact_boundary` message appears in the stream. Since summaries reduce information, specific initial instructions from the beginning of the conversation may be lost. The recommended rule is to store instructions in a memory file such as CLAUDE.md, which is reloaded with every request rather than relying on the initial prompt.

screens.outro: Now let's distinguish where subagents and Agent Skills are placed.

ext.title: Claude Code Docs, How the agent loop works
Anthropic Engineering, Effective context engineering for AI agents

screens.title: Location of Sub-Agents and Agent Skills
screens.lead: Select the “Subagent” and “Agent Skills” buttons alternately to compare the different problems the two devices solve.

states.label: subagent
states.body: Sub-agents are separate instances launched by the main agent. They begin with self-dialogue, hold intermediate results internally, and only return the final message. Benefits include parallel execution, specialized instructions, and tool limitations. Agents are defined via the `agents` parameter or files under `.claude/agents/`. The issue with this setup is that the main context becomes overloaded with intermediate results. For example, running style checks and security scans simultaneously results in the main agent accumulating only summaries of both inspections.

states.label: Agent Skills
states.body: Agent Skills are reusable, filesystem-based resources that grant Claude domain expertise. Once created, they are automatically used whenever relevant. While a prompt provides instructions for a single conversation, skills offer on-demand knowledge, eliminating the need to repeat the same guidance. The SDK automatically retrieves skills, commands, and memory from project `.claude/` and `~/.claude/` in a manner similar to Claude Code. The key issue this device resolves is the continuous consumption of context by repetitive procedures. In summary, subordinate agents isolate context, while skills control when context is added.

screens.outro: Let's take a single scene to examine when and how a skill is used.

screens.title: Skill behavior that "automatically" applies: the model opens the file upon viewing the explanation
screens.lead: When you select the highlighted section in the following scene, descriptions of each moment when the skill is activated in context appear. The formatting of the system prompt is provided as an illustrative example for clarity and may differ from the actual format.

The model's decision and actions

The code of the script is not uploaded to the context, only the execution output is uploaded..

marks.note: Metadata that always increases upon initialization—namely, name and description—is lightweight per skill, so it's safe to install many of them. The model determines whether a request requires a skill based solely on this description, so it must clearly specify both what the skill does and when it should be used.

screens.outro: Now let's take a closer look at the structure of skills from the perspective of progressive disclosure.

screens.title: Skills Structure: Three Stages of Progressive Disclosure
screens.lead: Please read the code alternately with the explanation on the right. This is an example code review skill directory and SKILL.md.

data.code:
code-review/
├── SKILL.md
├── report-template.md
├── team-rules.md
└── scripts/
    └── check_format.py

--- SKILL.md ---
---
name: code-review
description: Reviews a pull request according to team procedures and prepares a report. Used when requesting a code review or PR inspection.
---
# Code Review

## Procedure
1. First read the list of modified files.
2. Team rules are confirmed in [team-rules.md](team-rules.md).
3. The report follows the [report-template.md](report-template.md) format.
4. After writing, run scripts/check_format.py to verify the format.

notes.note: A skill is a directory containing instructions, executable code, and reference material. It is organized like an onboarding guide given to new team members. The premise of progressive disclosure is to separate procedures, forms, rules, and scripts into files.

Level 1 metadata is always loaded. The name and description of the SKILL.md header are entered in the system prompt at startup, so installing many skills is minimal. Since the description is the matching criterion, you must write both what the skill does and when it is used.

Step 2 instructions are procedures and best practices in the body of SKILL.md, which is loaded when a request is triggered by matching the description. The size recommended in the document is approximately less than 5,000 tokens.

Level 3 resources are loaded only when needed. Bundled reference files enter the context only when read, and scripts only enter the context when their output is executed. As a result, only the relevant content occupies the context at that moment.

Because skills contain instructions and executable code, a malicious skill can cause a model to make a tool call or execute code that is different from the skill's apparent purpose. Therefore, only use skills that you have created yourself or from trusted sources, and be especially careful with skills that import content from external URLs, as instructions in the imported content may be mixed. This is the same principle as the rule to connect only to trusted servers.

screens.outro: Let’s take a look at writing best practices to use your skills well.

screens.title: Best practices for writing skills
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term to see an explanation. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: The core of skill writing is conciseness. Since The context window is a public resource, only essential information is included, excluding any explanations that Claude already knows. The level of degree of freedom is adjusted according to the task's vulnerability. For context-based decisions, high-level degree of freedom is provided through written guidelines; if a preferred pattern exists, intermediate degree of freedom is given via parameterized scripts; for fragile and order-sensitive tasks, specific scripts are used to provide low-level degree of freedom. description specifies what is done and when it is used. Vague expressions such as "helps with documentation" are avoided. The SKILL.md body is kept under 500 lines, with longer content divided into reference files, and SKILL.md references those files via Direct link one level deep. For complex tasks, step-by-step workflows and feedback loop are included. Finally, all intended models are tested.

terms.term: The context window is a public resource
terms.tip: The content of a skill shares the same context window as conversations, other skills, and requests. Descriptions that the model already knows are subtracted because they just take up space.
This is the degree to which the model is allowed to make decisions autonomously. The greater the vulnerability of the work, the lower the degree of freedom and a specific script is set.
This is the criteria by which the skill is triggered. You need to capture both what the skill does and when it is used so it can be called at the right time.
This structure links directly from SKILL.md to the reference file. If a reference file points back to another reference file, there is a risk that only some of it will be read.
This is a method of incorporating a cycle of verifying and correcting the writing results into the procedure. Increase the quality of complex tasks.

screens.outro: Now that you have learned the concept, let's explain the example.

screens.title: Commentary 1: What happens when you turn repetitive procedures into skills?
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process of converting the code review agent to a skill in the first scene. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Start: Everything is at the system prompt.
steps.body: System prompts include review procedures, report forms, and team rules. You should read this every time, even if you ask questions unrelated to the code review. This cost accumulates as the number of conversations increases.

steps.title: Separation: Divide according to the nature of the content
steps.body: The procedures are in the body of SKILL.md, the report form and rule table are in the reference file, and the format verification is in the script. Since each piece of content is needed at a different time, dividing it into different files is a starting point. In this case, SKILL.md acts as a table of contents that links reference files directly one level in depth.

steps.title: Usual: only name and description in context
steps.body: By default, only the skill's name and description are available in the context. During conversations unrelated to reviews, neither the main content nor reference files are uploaded. This is why having multiple skills installed imposes little burden.

steps.title: When a review request comes
steps.body: If the review request matches the description, the body is loaded, and only the necessary reference files are read. The script is executed and only the output comes into the context. The script's code itself is not loaded into the context. When team rules are modified, management becomes easier as you only need to edit a single reference file.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Conversation outside of reviews rarely reduces context. Even in review conversations, I only write as much as I need. Once you create a procedure that has been pasted over and over again, it will be automatically used when relevant.

screens.outro: Next, let's compare how the skills and tools differ.

screens.title: Commentary 2: What is the difference between skills and tools?
screens.lead: Read the table to compare how tools and skills are handled differently in context.

data.caption: Comparison of tools and skills
rows: What does it contain
This is the action that the agent invokes. It actually does something, like reading a file, executing a command, or calling an external API.
It’s a bundle of knowledge on how to do it. Recall procedures, forms, and references when you need them.
How to get into context
Tool definitions are usually always in context.
They are loaded when needed in three steps: metadata, body, and resources.
run
It runs directly as a tool call.
Scripts in skills can be run as a tool (bash).
Relationship with MCP
MCP provides data connectivity with external tools.
A skill pairs with that tool by embodying the proper way to use it.
distinguishing question
If it “allows you to do something,” it is a tool.
“Does it tell you what to do?” is a skill.
Problems that arise when used incorrectly
If there are too many tools, definitions take over context and models become choppy.
If the description is ambiguous, it will not be called when needed or will be called at the wrong time.
When changes occur
Changing tools changes the scope of an agent's capabilities.
Just modifying the procedure document allows you to work in a different way with the same tools.
data.notes: The two devices work together rather than compete. For example, you can use MCP to connect to an issue tracker, and a skill to inform your team of issue creation rules. When judgment is difficult, separate the question from the last row of the table. Good design is a combination of tools that give you power and skills that teach you how to use them.

screens.outro: In the final commentary, we'll tie together sessions, subagents, and skills into one task.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Binding sessions, subagents, and skills into one task
screens.lead: The instructor explains how the three devices are tied together in a task called “Refactor the Certification Module and Fix the Tests.” Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: work
steps.body: The task is to “Refactor the authentication module and fix the tests.” Analysis, modification, and verification follow, and the method may need to be changed in the middle.

steps.title: Start with an analysis session
steps.body: First, we start the session with an analysis query. Start safely by only allowing reading tools. The agent reads the structure of the authentication module and records the results in the conversation history. Starting with read-only will prevent accidental file changes during the analysis phase.

steps.title: Continue to the same session
steps.body: Then send “Now change to JWT” to the same session. It carries over what you read earlier, so you don't have to read it from the beginning again. If only one conversation is in progress at a time in the same directory, continue is used, and if there are multiple sessions for each user, it is continued using resume.

steps.title: If you get stuck, fork
steps.body: If you get stuck, fork the session and try a different approach. The original session remains intact. Since file changes are not returned by the session, file checkpointing is also used. If the split session succeeds, the results are continued, and if it fails, it returns to the original session.

steps.title: Subagents and Skills
steps.body: Independent checks on style and security are distributed to subagents, sparing the main context. The team's review process is called a skill. Each of the three devices takes on different problems: memory, context isolation, and procedure reuse.

screens.outro: Finally, let's review the criteria for consolidating repeat instructions.

screens.title: Standards for organizing repeat instructions
screens.lead: Let's group the course content as a basis for summarizing repeat instructions. Please read it slowly.

paragraphs: If there are instructions to be appended each time, first ask yourself two questions: Is this required in every conversation, or is it only needed for specific requests? What is required in every conversation should be kept briefly in the system prompt or memory, while what is only needed for specific requests should be moved to a skill.

When moving content, divide it by nature. Procedures go into the main body, forms and rules into reference files, and fragile validations into scripts. The description contains everything about what to do and when to use it, so it can be retrieved at the correct time.

The memory of lengthy operations is delegated to sessions, blocked access is split and attempted via forks, and independent tasks that protect the main context are distributed among subordinate agents. Please remember that sessions store conversations but do not roll back files.
Start small and verify. Begin with one skill and one session, evaluate whether context utilization and result consistency have improved, then expand the scope.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Tools enable what can be done, and skills explain how to do it. The power of skills arises from being available only when needed, and in the required amount within the given context.

glossary.def: A library that provides tools like Claude Code, agent loops, and context management as code.
It is a record of conversations accumulated through an agent's work, containing prompts, tool calls, results, and responses.
This is an action to leave the original session as is and create a new session to try a different access.
It is a bundle of procedures and materials that are loaded when needed and is loaded in three stages: metadata, text, and resources.
This is a loading method that uploads only relevant content to the context at that time.
This is an action to free up space by converting old records into summaries before the window fills, which may result in the initial specific instructions being lost.

misconceptions.myth: The session also returns file changes.
misconceptions.fact: Sessions store conversations, not the filesystem. Files changed by the agent are restored separately using file checkpointing.

misconceptions.myth: Skill is another name for a tool.
misconceptions.fact: Tools are the actions that the agent performs, and skills are bundles of knowledge about how to do it. Scripts in skills can be run as tools.

misconceptions.myth: If you install a lot of skills, the context will become full.
misconceptions.fact: Only the name and description are loaded at startup, the body is loaded only when triggered, and references are loaded only when needed.

misconceptions.myth: When you resume a session, the model remembers previous conversations.
misconceptions.fact: The model only sees input per call. Resumption involves putting saved records back into the input, so the longer the record, the longer the input will be, and when the window fills up, older records can be replaced with summaries.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The Agent SDK lets you put tools and loops like Claude Code into your app using Python and TypeScript.
The agent loop iterates through judgment and tool execution until a response is made without a tool call.
A session is a record of a conversation. Continue, resume, and fork are used, and file changes are reverted separately.
Subagents work in an isolated context and return only a summary.
Skills are loaded in three stages: metadata, body, and resources to spare context, and are separated from tools by knowledge vs. actions.

closing.reflection: If I have instructions that I paste over and over again, what's the difference between those that I need all the time and those that I only need when I need them?
